Furthermore, this section provides a detailed analysis of the four types [of practice]. The initial text briefly judges that while practices differ, the principle remains the same;
it distinguishes [the "following one's own intention"] from the other three. Why? To clarify the obstacles that are thereby activated.
They are not the same, yet their principle and contemplation are no different.
Question:
One constantly sits and contemplates the three paths and so forth;
one constantly walks and contemplates the thirty-two marks of the Buddha and so forth;
and one practices the Vaipulya contemplation on the majestic countenance and ritual implements of the Honored One Mahāpratibhāna and so forth.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one contemplates a six-tusked white elephant and so forth;
in accordance with one's own intention, one contemplates the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
These four types of contemplation are each distinct.
What is meant by "similarity"? Answer:
This refers collectively to the objects experienced.
If one can contemplate that contemplation itself is nothing other than the single mind,
and that the principle of the object of focus is nothing other than the three truths,
then it may be said that the contemplation of principle is identical [to the contemplation of phenomena].
If one merely explains below that practice must rely on principle to penetrate phenomena,
yet fails to grasp the intent of the contemplation of principle,
it is not made clear that principle must be employed as the basis for phenomena.

Regarding the phrase "if the characteristics of the phenomena are inferior" and below: this is used to distinguish between "intervened" and "uninterrupted" in relation to the three [types of objects],
as the method is restricted to these three categories.
Regarding the three [categories], one distinguishes between the general and specific aspects of principle and phenomena.
In this regard, there is certainly no lack of method based on the sūtras;
moreover, all that is not subsumed under the three samādhis belongs herein.
It is not that methods are unnecessary here;
rather, these samādhis do not necessarily require specific methods.
Therefore, methods are restricted to the preceding three.
The question below distinguishes between the four samādhis as being with or without exhortation (*saprārthanā*);
the intent of the question is evident.
As for the intent of the answer:
Although this samādhi encompasses all sūtras and all virtues,
it is permitted that one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā even regarding unwholesome states; thus,
it protects those of dull faculties who do not understand the meaning of the texts.
Therefore, the direct explanation of contemplation does not explicitly encourage its cultivation.
If one were to rely on the preceding text to initiate and illuminate [the practice],
this would still involve initiating it while encouraging the cultivation of contemplation, rather than expressing the encouragement clearly and explicitly.
Therefore, viewed from the former perspective, it is called "without exhortation to practice.
However, according to various sutras, because it can extinguish grave offenses,
one must all the more exhort others to practice it, given the severity of such transgressions.
Therefore, as seen in the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*,
which states, "Sweep away filth and impurities so that they may attain purity," and as other sūtras provide similar examples, it is not entirely non-existent.
Below the Huai River, there were eminent masters who fell into the error of practicing [the Dharma] according to their own whims;
north of the Huai and north of the Yellow River,
those of false emptiness falsely claimed to be Mahāyāna followers.
Entering evil involves no contemplation;
therefore, it is illustrated by the metaphor of seizing a snake without restraint.
"Restraint" (jin) means to control.
This is because methods and regulations are used to control things.
Greed and desire are like snakes; observing the Dharma is like applying a spell.
To observe desire with observation is like seizing a snake.
The four propositions regarding unwholesome states are like the absence of prohibitions.

Although the bhikṣus admonished him three times, he did not desist.
They came and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Summon them."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him,
and he replied, "It is so."
The Buddha summoned the bhikṣus and questioned them.
The bhikṣus all replied,
"The Buddha has only said that desire is like fire, like a snake, like poison, and so forth."
The Buddha said,
"Because they have a perverted understanding.
It is like a person who, wishing to catch a snake for the purpose of traveling, goes about seeking that very snake."
In a quiet forest, he saw an extremely large snake;
he then seized the snake by its waist, causing it to turn around and raise its head,
which bit his hands, feet, and other limbs.
Because he has acquired an improper method for catching snakes, he experiences only extreme suffering;
the distorted understanding of the meaning is likewise so.
It is like wishing to properly catch a snake while grasping an iron staff with one's hand.
He saw an exceedingly large snake;
first pressing down its head with an iron staff and grasping its neck with his hand, the snake,
though it turned its tail back, merely coiled around his hands, feet, and other limbs.
It cannot further harm the person who has grasped the snake,
because that person is well-versed in the methods for handling snakes.
Likewise, it is the same now with one who enters into evil without contemplation.
To say that evil does not obstruct one is, on the contrary, to be harmed by evil.
If one enters the forest of the six sense-objects with the staff of sublime contemplation and encounters the snake of craving, one must press down its four heads.
Because they fail to seize [the mind] by the neck through contemplation, allowing the poison of affliction to reach the point of becoming physical karma,
they lose the pure, eternally abiding *dharmakāya*.
Those *āryas* lack the staff of right contemplation.
However, since it is taught that desire does not constitute an obstruction and the underlying meaning is largely the same, this analogy is borrowed here.

This refers to his former teacher,

If one does not cultivate skillfully,
one may temporarily allow unwholesome thoughts to arise that resemble the contemplation of emptiness,
and then mistakenly take this conceptual understanding of emptiness to be a profound realization.
This is the fault of practicing it oneself.
Not recognizing [the truth] and instructing others below [this level] is the fault of teaching others.

Chun was about to enter into a mistaken understanding of emptiness and teach it to others;

and they took his views as their authority.
That is to say, one considers only evil to be real;
from this point onward, even the understanding of emptiness is forgotten,
and one engages solely in the commission of all manner of evils.
The blind have no eye beneath them;
it is the fault of the disciples who mistakenly accept this that they lose [the vision].
Lacking the eye of the characteristics of instruction, they are called "blind."
Those who fail to cultivate virtue well are said to have dull faculties;
those who frequently give rise to desire are said to have heavy afflictions.
For such people, hearing further teachings from a teacher only serves to lead them further into evil.
Following their desires and inclinations, they commit all manner of evils,
thereby causing the common people to fall into ruin and bringing about the loss of both themselves and others.
To be negligent is to be reckless;

Gao Yao, the consort of Emperor Ku, became pregnant after treading upon the footprint of a divine being;
she considered it an ill omen and abandoned the child in a desolate lane, yet neither oxen nor sheep would tread upon him.
She placed it in cold water, where a bird shielded it with its wings;
Houyun, regarding it as a divine sign, took it and raised it.
When the child reached the age of childhood, he delighted in agriculture.

Shun then presented him to Yao.

This refers to the fact that from the times of the dynasties of Tang and Yu onwards, there were the Qiang, the Xianyun,
and the Xunyu, who dwelt on the northern borders of Heaven and moved about according to their herding and pasturing.
They migrate according to the availability of water and grass.
They have no plowed fields, but they possess livestock for breeding.
Each has their own designated territory, yet there are no written documents; they rely instead on verbal agreements and constraints.
The children are able to ride sheep and draw bows to shoot birds;
they practice only archery and lack propriety and righteousness.
From the sovereign downward, all consume the meat of livestock.
The young eat the rich and savory food, while the old eat what remains;
they honor the young and despise the old.
When the father dies, they take his wife as their own; when the elder brother dies, they take his wife as their own.
Since the Shang and Zhou dynasties, their incursions and plundering of the Middle Kingdom have been as unceasing as a continuous thread; during the Zhou dynasty,
they were so ravaged that their ancestral altars and state institutions were nearly extinguished.
Those who remained and were not fully subdued were like the silk threads [of the border].
Later, the Chief of the West (the King of Xi) campaigned against the Dog Rong and pursued them north of the Luo River;
they occasionally entered with tribute and were termed the "Frontier Submissions" (huangfu).

Exposing one's shoulders was a sign of the decline of the Zhou house;

heterodox teachers were like those wearing their upper garments bared;

The Biographies state:
"Ruan Ji, courtesy name Sizong."
He was a native of Weishi in Chenliu.
His appearance was imposing and his aspirations were grand and unrestrained;
he was haughtily independent, following his own nature without constraint.
He did not allow his joy or anger to be manifested on his countenance.
At times he would shut his door to read books for many days without coming out;
at other times he would ascend to the mountains and rivers, staying for two or three nights before forgetting to return home.
He was fond of wine and could whistle with such abandon that he would suddenly forget his physical form.
The people of the time mostly regarded him as a fool.
During the Jin and Wei eras, there were many famous scholars throughout the realm.
Yet those who remained whole were few;
consequently, he did not engage in worldly affairs and made habitual drinking to excess his constant practice.
This continued until Emperor Wen assisted in the governance of the state.
He was appointed as the Chancellor of Dongping.
He traveled there by ox-cart and returned within ten days;
though his nature and aspirations were filial, he did not adhere strictly to formal ritual decorum.
When his mother passed away, he was in the midst of playing a game of chess with someone;
when his opponent requested that he stop,
he insisted on staying to decide the wager.
Having finished gambling, he drank two sheng of wine;
raising his voice with a single cry,
he spat out several sheng of blood.
When Pei Kai went to offer his condolences,
[Dao’an] merely sat slumped in intoxication and stared straight ahead;
he looked upon those who followed conventional etiquette with "white eyes" (a look of disdain).
Consequently, those who followed conventional social customs viewed him with hostility as if he were an enemy.
At times, he would lie down beside the young wives of his neighbors;
at other times, when there was someone else who had died without relatives, he would go to offer his condolences.
The carriage did not follow the usual route;
when it reached its limit, they wailed and returned.

the sons and grandsons of the high officials followed their example.
Consequently, the Five Hu tribes invaded the country,
leading [the Emperor] to take refuge in Jiangdong;

Because of this, Emperor Hui’s third son, Rui, and others moved the capital to Jianye.

consequently, the dynasty’s mandate came to an end.

first, there arose the calamity of their jealousy toward the worthy.
Retreating from the world and feigning madness,
one later avoids the peril of being envied for one's talent;
why then need one emulate [Zhu] Dan?
Furthermore, there was Xian, the younger brother of Ruan Ji;
Xian’s second son was Fu.
During the reign of Emperor Yuan, Fu served as a military aide (canjun).
With disheveled hair, he drank wine and did not concern himself with royal affairs;
he was constantly subjected to reprimands by the Right Minister,
yet the Emperor tolerated him.
Later, he was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Changshi) of Yangzhou.

When he first ascended the throne, he also believed in the Buddha-dharma;

Having personally received the talismans and registers,

Yuansong’s views were in accord with the Emperor, who accepted his words;

nor provide partial security for those of the Two Vehicles or the Five Classics.

King Wu of Zhou was thus a Tathāgata;
he used his capital city to build monasteries for the Saṃgha and brought together husbands and wives to serve as the holy assembly.
He promoted those of superior virtue to serve as the three pillars of governance;
he followed the elders as his presiding seniors;

for each individual quality, three qualities are further distinguished.
As with the body, so it is with the other two.
Why? For how could there be an arising of the response without these two qualities?
The same applies to the other two [bodies].
As for "ceasing transformation," it refers to manifesting entry into nirvana once the conditions for transformation have been exhausted.
This indicates returning to the secret treasury of the three virtues.
Next, regarding the inconceivable,
its meaning is largely the same as the preceding general and specific [explanations].
However, it does not separately list the names of the three bodies, the three wisdoms, and the three liberations;
it simply refers to them as "body," "non-body," and so forth. Why is this so?
This clarifies that the preceding general and specific [categories] are all mutually identical.
Furthermore, in various sūtras and śāstras, there are times when the body (kāya) and non-body (akāya), etc., are directly named;
this is because a single virtue possesses the three virtues, which is inconceivable.
Next, regarding the interpretation of the meaning of the "inconceivable" (*acintya*) by way of the sequence of phenomena and principle from beginning to end:
this also proceeds first with a general overview and subsequently with specific details.
First, as for the general overview: it generally concerns the three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) and the three virtues (*guṇa*), which, in their mutual relationship, are non-different yet different.
If explained according to principle, virtue and its obstacles are non-dual, and there is neither new nor old.

However, if explained according to phenomena, the name "obstacle" is not new because it refers to that which is originally present; the name "virtue" is not old because it refers to that which is acquired through cultivation.
Since phenomena and principle are non-dual yet dual within their non-duality,
every single phrase states that they are neither new nor old, yet are both new and old.
Because this is established in terms of what is attained through cultivation, the name is designated based on its meritorious qualities.
Because they are established based on their intrinsic nature, they are termed the "three obstacles.
Therefore, there exists that which obstructs and that which is obstructed;
there is the fundamental existence, the present existence, and the final existence with its beginning.
If one speaks according to principle, there is neither subject nor object, nor even beginning nor end.
Furthermore, in the passage below [the text] specifically correlates the three delusions with the three virtues.
If one understands the general and specific aspects of reaching the lower and binding the upper,
the mention of "vertical and horizontal," "opening and closing," and so forth,
serves as an illustration.
In the arrangement of the sequence, the Dharma-body must come first; next comes Prajñā;
and finally, Liberation.
Therefore, it is called "vertical" (zòng).
When analyzed according to their meanings, each one is further divided into three;
therefore, it is called "horizontal" (héng).
It is also called "opening.
Since the three [periods] are one, it is called "joining.
Taking the arousal of the mind as the beginning.
"Ultimate" refers to the end.
Furthermore, the Deer Park is the beginning and the Twin Trees are the end.
In this manner, there is a horizontal unfolding and closing of the beginning and the end.
All of these should be explained through their modes of activity (*lakṣaṇa*) by means of such concepts as the inconceivable, the new, and the old;
therefore it is said that "the examples are all thus.
Next, regarding the explanation based on the two characters of the "ultimate aim" (*zhìguī*):
That which points toward and that to which one returns are the teachings of the three virtues;
that which is pointed toward and that which is returned to are the principles of the three virtues.
Therefore, this further type of interpretation is provided.
"Regarding 'The ultimate aim is the three virtues,' below this,
the various names are unified.
Since the three virtues already encompass all phenomena, [they serve as the comprehensive designation]."
Therefore, one must synthesize all these various names.
This should be understood as the concluding summary:
"characteristics" refers to the Dharmakāya, and "teaching" refers to Prajñāpāramitā.
Power is itself liberation.
Regarding the statement that each of the three virtues is "various," it means that within each individual virtue, all phenomena are fully present.
Because they mutually encompass one another, they are called "various.
Although they are called various, they do not transcend the single secret treasury of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
Not only are the dharma-gates fully subsumed within these three virtues; [all else is likewise contained therein].
That which is manifested through the modes of transformation also does not exceed three:
as in the *Avataṃsaka*, Vairocana is the Dharmakāya,
and Śākyamuni is Prajñā.
Śākyamuni is liberation;
the Buddha is prajñā;
the platform is the dharmakāya.
Sitting is itself liberation.
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, it is said that when he thought of himself lying ill upon his bed,
the bed was itself the Dharma-body.
Sleeping is *prajñā* (wisdom);
illness is *vimokṣa* (liberation);
for the bed is that upon which one relies.
Sleep is that which accords with reality;
illness is a manifestation. Thus it is said in the Prajñā[pāramitā]:
The body is the Dharma-body;
the light is Prajñā;
the teaching is Liberation.
In the Lotus Sutra,
the robe is the Dharmakāya and the seat is Prajñā.
The chamber is itself liberation.
Furthermore, the fundamental reality is the Dharmakāya,
while its manifestations are liberation.
The fundamental non-duality is itself Prajñā.
Regarding the correct elucidation of the three virtues within Nirvāṇa, it has already been explained as before.
As for that which is signified:
The four withered aspects are prajñā;
the four flourishing aspects are liberation;
that which is neither is the dharmakāya.
Regarding such a fundamental aim, if even the Buddhas have not yet fully realized it, Bodhisattvas still remain obscure about it;
how much more so for those of the Two Vehicles!
Now, as we dwell in this age of the Semblance Dharma and behold these true texts, [we are fortunate].

Were it not for those who have planted wondrous causes in past lives, this would truly be difficult to encounter; how much more so when the Ten Vehicles and Ten Objects originate from the Single House (the Tiantai school), and the Ten Realms and Ten Non-Realms are distinctions not made by others.
Without these as standards for teaching and practice, what could one take as the ultimate goal?
Furthermore, for instance, while the intentions of the Six Sects are largely the same,
the expositions of the Nine Schools differ slightly;
Zhuangzi returns [all things] to spontaneity (*zì'ěr*).
Laozi specifically lamented the abandonment of luxury;
how much more so when the sacrifice of horses and the boiling of rams invite the three evils,
and the offering of dried meat and millet leads to conflagrations.
Such is the ultimate goal toward which one tends; it is not far off,
yet it does not even reach the realms of humans and devas— how much less could it concern the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) of the Tripitaka or Shared Teachings?
According to their respective calculations, how could they know that whatever is spoken is entirely of one undifferentiated nature?
May all who encounter this teaching give rise to a heart of profound joy, aspiring to hear it again in future lives and swiftly realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
